title: Who Has Seen the Wind?
author: Christina Rossetti
intro: Two stanzas, eight lines. The poem is almost a riddle — it asks a question, admits the answer is 'no one,' and then tells you how to see what you can't see. Watch how the second stanza mirrors the first with tiny variations.
passage:
Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling,
The wind is passing through.

Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads,
The wind is passing by.

annotations.note: STR: the opening question is also the title. The poem will answer this question indirectly, by showing the wind's effects rather than the wind itself.
E: this line directly answers the question. Nobody in the poem has seen the wind, so the rest of the poem must prove the wind through visible effects.
INF: "Leaves hang trembling" is the visible clue that lets us infer the invisible wind’s presence.
TH: The poem’s quiet central idea lands here: an unseen force can be known by its visible effects.
STR: second stanza repeats the question — same words, new context. The repetition is the poem's structural form; the learning is in watching what changes underneath.
STR: this mirrors and slightly varies 'Neither I nor you' from stanza 1 — the pronouns swap order. The poem keeps gently shifting its surface under the repetition.
FIG: The trees are personified as if they have heads and can bow. This image supports the inference that we know wind by what it moves.
STR: first stanza says 'passing through'; second stanza says 'passing by.' One small phrase changes, so the poem's repeated structure moves with the wind.

discussion_prompts: The poem repeats almost the same words in stanzas 1 and 2 — but not exactly. Find every tiny difference. Why each change?
Why does Rossetti show leaves trembling and trees bowing instead of only saying "the wind is there"?
What is this poem REALLY about? Just wind, or something bigger? Defend your answer.
How does the repeated two-stanza structure help the poem teach its idea?
discussion_answers: Differences: (a) 'I nor you' → 'you nor I' (pronouns swap); (b) 'leaves hang trembling' → 'trees bow down their heads' (smaller plants → bigger plants; smaller motion → bigger motion); (c) 'passing through' → 'passing by' (direction changes). Each variation makes the wind feel bigger and the world more affected.
Because the poem’s method is indirect proof: we cannot see wind itself, but we can read its effects in the world.

Plausible deeper readings: God (an invisible force known only through visible effects); time; emotion; any unseen power. The poem teaches a reading habit — look for what something DOES, not just what it IS. That habit applies far beyond wind.
The repeated question and denial create a pattern, while the changed effects, from trembling leaves to bowing trees, show the same invisible force becoming knowable in different visible ways.
